# Run comparison view (side-by-side and diff) for training and pipeline runs

## Description

This epic delivers a run comparison view in the Dashboard: users select two or
more training or Data Science Pipelines runs and view their parameters and
metrics side by side, including a diff presentation that highlights which
parameters and metrics changed between two selected runs. Today, parameters
and metrics live only on per-run pages, forcing comparison into exported
spreadsheets; this epic brings that comparison into the platform console.

## Scope

- Multi-select of runs from the existing runs list in the Dashboard.
- A comparison view presenting the selected runs' parameters and metrics side
  by side.
- A diff presentation of the same comparison surface that highlights which
  parameters and metrics changed between two selected runs (a presentation
  mode of the side-by-side view, not a separate surface).
- The comparison works for both training runs and Data Science Pipelines
  runs: run parameters and metrics are read through the run surfaces the
  Dashboard already consumes. No Data Science Pipelines code changes are
  expected; validation that pipeline runs compare correctly is in the
  acceptance criteria below.
- No changes to automatic run selection, promotion, cross-cluster, or
  cross-project comparison (strategy out of scope).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given two or more runs selected from the runs list, when the user opens the
  comparison, then the parameters and metrics of all selected runs are
  displayed side by side in the Dashboard.
- Given two runs presented in the comparison view, the parameters and metrics
  that differ between them are visually highlighted (diff view).
- The comparison works for Data Science Pipelines runs as well as training
  runs, using existing run metadata access (passive validation of the Data
  Science Pipelines component — if existing access proves insufficient, the
  gap is raised as follow-up scope rather than silently dropped).
- Existing per-run pages continue to function without regression.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): users can select two or more runs and view their parameters and
  metrics side by side in the Dashboard.
- HLR-3 (P1): run "diff" view highlighting which parameters and metrics
  changed between two selected runs — a presentation mode of the same
  comparison surface as HLR-1, consolidated into this epic at the higher
  priority (the strategy notes its requirements were consolidated from two
  customer councils with overlapping wording).

# Producing-run lineage on registered model versions

## Description

This epic makes registered model versions in the Model Registry carry a
resolvable reference to the run that produced them, so model promotion
decisions can trace a candidate version back to its training or pipeline run.
It delivers the lineage data and exposes it through the registry's API for
consumption by the registry UI and other clients.

## Scope

- Capture the producing-run reference when a model version is registered from
  a run, using the model-version metadata extension point (custom properties
  on ModelVersion entities).
- Expose the producing-run reference through the Model Registry REST API so
  the registry UI can resolve it.
- Backward compatibility: existing model versions without a producing-run
  reference remain valid.
- Out of scope: automatic best-run selection or promotion, and comparison
  across clusters or projects (strategy out of scope).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a model version registered from a run, the version carries a
  resolvable reference to the run that produced it.
- The producing-run reference is retrievable through the Model Registry REST
  API.
- Model versions registered before this change (no producing-run reference)
  remain readable and valid through the API and UI.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P1): registered model versions link back to the run that produced
  them (data and API half of the requirement; the registry-UI affordance that
  opens a comparison is delivered by the Dashboard-side epic).

# Open run comparison from the Model Registry UI

## Description

This epic adds the affordance in the registry UI (surfaced in the Dashboard)
to open the run comparison for a registered model version's linked producing
run, completing the path from model promotion back to experiment evidence.
It builds on two capabilities: the run comparison view for training and
pipeline runs, and the producing-run reference carried by registered model
versions in the Model Registry.

## Scope

- An action on the registered model version view in the registry UI that
  opens the run comparison seeded with the model version's linked producing
  run.
- Graceful degradation for model versions that carry no producing-run
  reference (the action is hidden or disabled).
- Out of scope: comparison across clusters or projects, and automatic
  best-run selection or promotion (strategy out of scope).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a registered model version that carries a producing-run reference,
  the registry UI offers an action that opens the run comparison view with
  that run included.
- Given a registered model version without a producing-run reference, the
  registry UI presents no broken or misleading entry point to the comparison.
- The opened comparison presents the linked run's parameters and metrics
  identically to the same run opened from the runs list.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P1): "so a comparison can be opened from the Model Registry" — the
  registry-UI half of the requirement, delivered in the Dashboard because the
  registry UI is a Dashboard surface.

If Step 0 produced a below-threshold or docs-only result, the strategy is already a single epic — do not apply priority-split logic.\n93\t\n94\t- Each P0/P1/P2 requirement must map to one or more epics\n95\t- Every HLR must be covered — no orphaned requirements\n96\t- Priority inheritance: prerequisite epic inherits the highest priority of all HLRs it transitively enables\n97\t- An epic blocking all P0 work is implicitly P0\n98\t- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is \"distinct and deferrable\" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries.\n99\t- **Redundant / overlapping HLRs — consolidate, never split:** strategies merged from multiple sources sometimes state one capability twice in different words (e.g. \"select two or more runs and view their parameters and metrics side by side\" and \"a diff view highlighting which parameters and metrics changed between two selected runs\" — the diff view is a presentation mode of the same comparison surface over the same run data). When two HLRs describe the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint for the same component and team — one a restatement or presentation mode of the other — they are ONE capability: cover both with a single epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLR ids, at the higher of the two priorities. Do not split them into separate epics by priority label: on a shared surface a P0/P1 pair is redundant wording, not a deferral signal, and splitting produces two epics building the same surface plus an artificial serialization edge between them — a boundary violation even when the second epic only extends the first's surface.\n100\t- `docs-authoring` priority exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance. They do not push their priority upstream to the implementations they depend on. Instead, derive their priority from the strategy frontmatter `priority` field: Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2. If the field is missing or empty, default to P2.\n101\t\n102\t## Step 5: Build Dependency DAG\n103\t\n104\tApply these rules to construct edges between epics:\n105\t\n106\t### Epic Boundary Rules\n107\t1. Different component OR different team → separate epics\n108\t2. Same component + same team + same logical change → single epic. When splitting within a single component, split along two axes:\n109\t   - **Architectural sub-system boundaries**: backend API vs. frontend plugin, Go service vs. React UI, etc.\n110\t   - **Work-product type boundaries**: code implementation, content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), and documentation are different kinds of work — they require different skills, different review criteria, and produce different PR review cycles. An epic that mixes code implementation with content authoring should be split even if the same team owns both. **Exception — incidental documentation touch-ups:** updating captions, screenshots, or references that fall out of a code change (no new content authored) is not a separate work stream — fold it into the originating epic as scope/acceptance criteria rather than a standalone `docs-authoring` epic. Only substantive content/documentation authoring (new tutorials, sample notebooks, curated examples, new or rewritten doc topics), or a strategy with `Documentation Support: Yes`, warrants a separate epic.\n111\t   These axes take precedence when deciding where to draw epic boundaries within a component. Step 4 may additionally split by priority when features are genuinely deferrable — but the initial boundary structure should come from architecture and work-product type, not from walking down the HLR list. Never split such that two epics must build the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint independently.\n112\t\n113\t### Investigation Edges\n114\t3. Investigation determines scope/existence of downstream work → blocking edge to all affected Implementations. Every downstream epic gated by an Investigation is a true gate (`remove` if the epic may not exist, `rewrite` if scope/approach changes, `add_remediation` if the investigation may reveal a problem requiring additional work) — record this in Step 8b when writing frontmatter. Bounded outcomes (≤3): conditional branches. Unbounded: phased decomposition.\n115\t4. Investigation is informational only (doesn't change what gets built) → not a true Investigation. Reclassify as an acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic, or as an Implementation that produces a deliverable.\n116\t\n117\t### Implementation Type Ordering\n118\t5. `repo-onboarding` → `konflux-onboarding` always serial (pipeline needs repo)\n119\t6. `repo-onboarding` → general implementation of onboarded component always serial (code needs repo). That coupling is enforced by the Rule 25 \"build pipeline green\" AC on the general implementation epic, never by a DAG dependency. A `konflux-onboarding → general` edge serializes work that must run in parallel and is a rule violation. This holds for EVERY `konflux-onboarding` × general-implementation pair in the decomposition, whatever the general epic's component or deliverable — a stack-wide assembly, packaging, or evidence epic that consumes the pipeline's outputs is still a general implementation. Strategy replaces existing capability → add rollback/feature-flag AC to replacing Implementation epic\n145\t24. `docs-authoring` epic → add \"technically reviewed against implementation\" AC\n146\t25. Implementation with `konflux-onboarding` in dependency chain → add \"build pipeline green\" AC\n147\t\n148\t## Step 5.5: Detect Tiered Delivery\n149\t\n150\tWhen an external dependency has uncertain timing:\n151\t\n152\t1. Can the strategy deliver partial value without it?\n153\t2. **YES** → Split into:\n154\t   - **Tier 1**: Independent work (user-facing features OR risk-reduction spikes/validations)\n155\t   - **Tier 2**: Dependency-gated work (blocked by upstream epic)\n156\t3. **NO** → Linear dependencies; external dependency blocks all downstream\n157\t\n158\t## Step 6: Classify Epics\n159\t\n160\tFor each epic, determine:\n161\t\n162\t### Type (mandatory)\n163\t- **Implementation**: Produce an artifact (code, config, docs, manifests, pipelines, RFCs, upstream PRs)\n164\t- **Investigation**: Resolve uncertainty (answer a question or make a decision that other epics depend on)\n165\t\n166\t### Implementation Type (optional routing label)\n167\t\n168\t| Label | When to apply |\n169\t|-------|--------------|\n170\t| `docs-authoring` | Red Hat docs content process — specialized tooling |\n171\t| `konflux-onboarding` | Build pipeline onboarding — known-recipe |\n172\t| `license-validation` | License scanning for transitive dependencies |\n173\t| `repo-onboarding` | Midstream repo fork creation under opendatahub-io |\n174\t| _(absent/null)_ | General-purpose — read target repo, figure it out |\n175\t\n176\t### AI Implementability Signals\n177\t\n178\tScore signals so the pipeline can compute an AI-implementability classification deterministically. **Do not compute the total score or classification yourself.** Use the signal set that matches the epic `type` — Implementation and Investigation epics measure different things.\n179\t\n180\t#### Implementation epics → `ai_signals` (9 signals)\n181\t\n182\tEvaluate each as +1 (favorable), 0 (neutral/N/A), or -1 (unfavorable). Write the values into `ai_signals`.\n183\t\n184\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | +1 Condition | -1 Condition |\n185\t|---|--------|----------------|-------------|-------------|\n186\t| 1 | Change specificity | `change_specificity` | Exact file paths, API endpoints, field names known | Vague scope (\"improve X\") |\n187\t| 2 | Pattern precedent | `pattern_precedent` | Similar changes exist in same codebase | No precedent in codebase |\n188\t| 3 | Adapter/plugin pattern | `adapter_pattern` | Follows existing reference implementation | N/A (0 if absent) |\n189\t| 4 | Existing foundation | `existing_foundation` | Extending existing code/feature | Greenfield, no foundation |\n190\t| 5 | Open questions | `open_questions` | All design decisions resolved for this epic | Open questions that would change implementation approach |\n191\t| 6 | External dependency | `external_dependency` | None | Upstream contribution or vendor coordination needed |\n192\t| 7 | Human process gates | `human_process_gates` | None | Requires human approval step |\n193\t| 8 | Repo access | `repo_access` | AI can clone and modify target repo | Repo inaccessible or special access required |\n194\t| 9 | Architecture claims | `architecture_claims` | Epic's scope or the strategy's premise about the component (surfaces, repos, deployment model, maturity state such as Tech Preview/GA) is corroborated by an architecture-context file — name that file in the rationale | Strategy asserts architecture that the context files contradict or cannot back |\n195\t\n196\t**Scoring `architecture_claims` (signal 9):** a strategy makes architecture claims whenever it states what a component IS — its maturity state (\"shipped as Tech Preview\", \"generally available\"), its CRD/API/repo surfaces, its deployment model — even when it never uses the word \"claim\". A strategy premise that drives the decomposition (e.g. a maturity gap motivating a hardening program) is an architecture claim. Check `.context/architecture-context/` for the epic's components: score +1 when a context file corroborates the premise or grounds the epic's scope, and cite that file in the rationale; score -1 when the strategy asserts something the context contradicts; score 0 only when no context file covers any component the epic touches. \"The strategy makes no specific architecture claims\" is not a valid 0 rationale when context files exist for the components in scope.\n197\t\n198\t#### Investigation epics → `investigation_signals` (5 signals)\n199\t\n200\t**Do not use the 9 Implementation signals for Investigation epics.** Those penalize the *defining* traits of an investigation (open questions, no prior foundation, external dependency), so they mis-route nearly every investigation to Low — even ones the AI resolves easily. Instead score these five, which predict whether the AI investigation skill can resolve the unknowns (→ assign to the skill) or a person must (→ assign to a person). Write the values into `investigation_signals`.\n201\t\n202\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | Range | How to score |\n203\t|---|--------|-----------------|-------|--------------|\n204\t| 1 | Question specificity | `question_specificity` | -1 / 0 / +1 | +1 concrete, enumerable questions with a defined pass/fail criterion; -1 vague or criterion undefined (a human must frame it first) |\n205\t| 2 | Source accessibility | `source_accessibility` | 0 / +1 | +1 a readable artifact that **contains or determines the answer** exists (open repo, docs, public record). 0 when the only readable material does **not** hold the answer — e.g. a decision/PR still under review (the answer doesn't exist yet) |\n206\t| 3 | Local runnability | `local_runnability` | 0 / +1 | +1 the components can be exercised as a downloaded **binary or pip/npm library** locally — including backing a datastore with an embedded/bundled server (e.g. `pgserver` for PostgreSQL). 0 only if it genuinely can't run without a container/cluster |\n207\t| 4 | Cluster/hardware dependence | `cluster_hardware_dependence` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 some *peripheral* questions need a live cluster / GPU / prod-scale. -2 a *gating* question does. **What an operator/controller _generates_** (rendered CR, template, NetworkPolicy, RBAC in its source repo) is readable source — score it under `source_accessibility`, **not** here; only the *as-deployed runtime state* of a live cluster counts as a dependence |\n208\t| 5 | Human judgment required | `human_judgment_required` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 a *peripheral* question needs a stakeholder/product decision or external-party input. -2 the *gating* question is itself a human/governance decision or external coordination the AI cannot make (e.g. \"is this ADR approved?\") |\n209\t\n210\tThe pipeline routes: **High** → assign to the investigation skill; **Medium** → hybrid (skill resolves the desk/local parts and hands a spec to a human for the rest); **Low** → assign to a person.\n211\t\n212\tWrite the signal rationale to a separate file `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN-ai-signals.md` (one per epic), for whichever signal set you used. Format as a markdown table with Signal, Value, and Rationale columns. Do not write the signals table into the epic body.\n213\t\n214\t## Step 6.5: Health Warnings\n215\t\n216\t### Non-blocking warnings (decomposition proceeds, human verifies later)\n217\t- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)\n218\t- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent\n219\t\n220\t### Handling unclear strategy passages\n221\t\n222\tWhen the strategy is unclear about something, apply this two-way distinction:\n223\t\n224\t| Situation | Handling |\n225\t|-----------|---------|\n226\t| **Implementation detail** — the team will resolve this when they start the work (version choices, API surface discovery, config decisions, validation of assumptions) | Not a flag. Capture as an AC on the relevant epic if needed. Most unclear passages fall here. |\n227\t| **Genuine unknown** — nobody knows yet, resolution requires technical work, and the answer changes which downstream epics exist or what they do | Investigation epic with conditional downstream epics. |\n228\t\n229\tWhen a strategy explicitly flags something as an open question, pending review, or conditional ADR, treat it as a genuine unknown — the strategy author has already classified it. Do not downgrade to an implementation detail based on descriptive text elsewhere in the strategy. A detailed description of current state is context, not a decision. If the strategy indicates the resolution could require a different approach (conditional ADRs, \"if X requires changes to Y\"), evaluate which downstream epics build on the current assumption and gate them on the resolution.\n230\t\n231\t## Step 7: Derive Acceptance Criteria\n232\t\n233\tEach epic gets acceptance criteria derived from:\n234\t- Strategy acceptance criteria allocated to this epic's scope\n235\t- HLRs mapped to this epic\n236\t- Implementation-specific requirements (build pipeline green, rollback plan, doc review, etc.)\n237\t- Rules 23-25 from Step 5\n238\t\n239\tEvery AC must be a testable pass/fail condition on THIS epic's own deliverable — something the epic's engineering work produces or verifies. Externally-controlled preconditions are not ACs, in either form: schedule constraints (turnaround you do not control — accredited-lab queues, review-board cadence, upstream vendor timing) or availability preconditions (procurement, dedicated hardware or node allocation, partner-lab access, environment provisioning) — anything granted by parties outside the strategy belongs in the epic's Risks/Notes or the summary's Health Warnings. Write the AC at the engineering completion point you do control — \"the evidence package is submitted to the certification lab and triaged\" is a valid AC; \"lab scheduling and review-board cadence are externally controlled and cannot be compressed\" is a schedule-risk note misfiled as an AC; \"dedicated hardware nodes are available to the campaign\" is an availability precondition misfiled as an AC — the epic's work may include *securing* access, but the access being granted is not a condition the epic's deliverable produces, so it stays in Risks/Notes while the AC sits on the deliverable itself (e.g. the campaign's validated report).\n240\t\n241\t## Step 8: Generate Artifacts\n242\t\n243\t### Step 8a: Write decomposition summary (the plan)\n244\t\n245\tWrite the decomposition summary **first** — this is the blueprint for all epic files.\n246\t\n247\tWrite `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md` in two steps:\n248\t\n249\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections:\n250\t   - **Epic List** (table: ID, title, type, team, priority)\n251\t   - **Dependency DAG** (Mermaid `graph TD` diagram — roots at top, arrows point from dependency to dependent: `E001 --> E003` means \"E001 must complete before E003 can start\")\n252\t   - **DAG Justification** (table: edge, rule, rationale)\n253\t   - **HLR Traceability Matrix** (HLR → epic mapping, confirming full coverage)\n254\t   - **Health Warnings** (priority inversions, scope traps — if any)\n255\t   - **Tiered Delivery** (if applicable — Tier 1 vs Tier 2 split)\n256\t\n257\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n258\t\n259\t```bash\n260\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md \\\n261\t    parent_strat=\"{ID}\" epic_count=<N> critical_path_length=<N>\n262\t```\n263\t\n264\tAdd `triage=<value> triage_rationale=\"<reason>\"` for triaged strategies (Step 0).\n265\t\n266\t### Scope constraint: decompose, don't design\n267\t\n268\tYour job is to break strategy scope into units of work, not to make implementation decisions.\n269\tIf the strategy describes a capability at a functional level, the epic scope stays at that level.\n270\tDo not invent API paths, URL schemas, response formats, environment variables, caching policies,\n271\tCRD field names, or other implementation details not stated in the strategy. Those are decisions\n272\tfor the implementing team.\n273\t\n274\t### Step 8b: Write per-epic files\n275\t\n276\tWrite one file per epic to `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN.md` (e.g., `{ID}-E001.md`, `{ID}-E002.md`), following the decomposition summary as the plan. Each epic's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, and HLR mappings must match what the summary specifies.\n277\t\n278\tFor each epic, write in two steps:\n279\t\n280\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections (minimum — add additional sections when the strategy contains relevant content for this epic's scope, e.g., risks, assumptions, open questions, stakeholder commitments):\n281\t   - **Title** (one line)\n282\t   - **Description** (what this epic delivers)\n283\t   - **Scope** (specific changes in this epic)\n284\t   - **Acceptance Criteria** (derived from strategy)\n285\t   - **HLR Traceability** (which strategy HLRs this epic covers)\n286\t   The four section headings are literal and required for EVERY epic, including `docs-authoring` epics — an outline of content topics goes INSIDE the `## Scope` section, never as a renamed `## Content Outline` heading (a renamed heading fails the artifact contract).\n287\t   Signal rationales go in a separate file (see Step 6) — do not include them in the epic body.\n288\t\n289\t   **No cross-references to sibling epics.** Do not reference other epics by draft ID (e.g., \"E001\", \"E003\") anywhere in the body — not in descriptions, scope, acceptance criteria, or HLR traceability. Draft IDs are internal to the decomposition and meaningless once epics are created in Jira. Dependency relationships are captured by frontmatter `dependencies` and Jira Blocks links. Each epic body must be self-contained: describe what it delivers and depends on in plain terms (e.g., \"the OTEL env var injection capability\" not \"E003\") without naming sibling epics.\n290\t\n291\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n292\t\n293\t```bash\n294\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \\\n295\t    epic_id=\"{ID}-E001\" title=\"<epic title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n296\t    component=\"<canonical name from .context/rhai-components.txt>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n297\t    type=Implementation priority=P0 \\\n298\t    dependencies=\"{ID}-E002,{ID}-E003\" \\\n299\t    ai_signals.change_specificity=1 \\\n300\t    ai_signals.pattern_precedent=1 \\\n301\t    ai_signals.adapter_pattern=0 \\\n302\t    ai_signals.existing_foundation=1 \\\n303\t    ai_signals.open_questions=-1 \\\n304\t    ai_signals.external_dependency=0 \\\n305\t    ai_signals.human_process_gates=-1 \\\n306\t    ai_signals.repo_access=1 \\\n307\t    ai_signals.architecture_claims=1\n308\t```\n309\t\n310\tFor an **Investigation** epic, set `type=Investigation` and write the five\n311\t`investigation_signals` instead of `ai_signals` (do not set both):\n312\t\n313\t```bash\n314\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \\\n315\t    epic_id=\"{ID}-E001\" title=\"<epic title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n316\t    component=\"<canonical name>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n317\t    type=Investigation priority=P0 \\\n318\t    investigation_signals.question_specificity=1 \\\n319\t    investigation_signals.source_accessibility=1 \\\n320\t    investigation_signals.local_runnability=1 \\\n321\t    investigation_signals.cluster_hardware_dependence=0 \\\n322\t    investigation_signals.human_judgment_required=0\n323\t```\n324\t\n325\tAdd optional fields only when non-null: `implementation_type=<value>`, `branch=<value>`, `gated_by=<epic_id>`, `gate_failure_impact.action=<value> gate_failure_impact.fallback_approach=\"<text>\"`. Every epic that depends on an Investigation should have `gated_by` pointing to that Investigation (see Rule 3).\n326\t\n327\tDo **not** include `ai_implementability` or `ai_implementability_score` — the pipeline computes those from `ai_signals` (Implementation) or `investigation_signals` (Investigation) automatically.\n328\t\n329\t### Step 8c: Verify consistency\n330\t\n331\tAfter writing all epic files, run:\n332\t```\n333\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py batch-read artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-*E[0-9][0-9][0-9].md\n334\t```\n335\t\n336\tCompare the output against the decomposition summary. If any epic file's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, or HLR mappings diverged from the plan, fix the epic file to match the summary.\n337\t\n338\tThen run the contract validator until it passes:\n339\t\n340\t```bash\n341\tpython3 skills/epic-decompose/scripts/validate_decomposition.py {ID}\n342\t```\n343\t\n344\tIt deterministically checks what downstream consumers enforce and an LLM step can silently get wrong: epic body sections (Description / Scope / Acceptance Criteria / HLR Traceability), `component` values verbatim in `.context/rhai-components.txt`, Rule 11 (docs-authoring blocked by every Implementation epic), priority inheritance (an epic blocking P0 work is itself P0), and implementation-type parallelism (Rules 7/8/10 — no `dependencies` edge, in either direction, between `license-validation` and `repo-onboarding`, `license-validation` and `konflux-onboarding`, or `konflux-onboarding` and a general implementation; a flagged edge is removed from the dependent epic's `dependencies` and its coupling expressed as an AC gate instead). It prints one `VIOLATION:` line per problem and exits non-zero. Fix every violation by editing the epic files (never edit the script), re-run, and proceed only once it prints `OK`.\n345\t\n346\tThen, as your **final action** — after every epic file is written, any divergence is fixed, and the validator prints `OK` — mark the decomposition complete:\n347\t\n348\t```\n349\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md decompose_complete=true\n350\t```\n351\t\n352\tThe pipeline uses this field to detect that you have finished. Until it is set, the review agent is not launched.
